content: Silphium laciniatum, commonly known as Compass Flower, Compass Plant, or Rosinweed, is a species of flowering plant that belongs to the genus Silphium. It is indigenous to the east-central regions of North America, with its range extending from southern Ontario and New York in the north, down to Alabama in the south, and westward across the prairies to North Dakota and Colorado, reaching as far south as Texas. This plant is a perennial herbaceous species that bears a resemblance to sunflowers. It typically grows to a height of 1 to 4 meters and is characterized by stems that are covered in bristly hairs. The leaves of the plant are arranged alternately along the stem and are deeply lobed in a pinnate fashion. The basal leaves can reach lengths of up to 40 centimeters, while the leaves higher up the stem are progressively smaller. The flowers of Silphium laciniatum are borne in capitula, or flowerheads, which range in diameter from 5 to 12 centimeters. Each flowerhead consists of a ring of ray florets encircling a central cluster of disc florets, with the disc florets measuring approximately 2 to 3 centimeters in diameter. The plant typically blooms in late summer, with its flowering period occurring from July to September. The name Compass Plant is derived from the unique orientation of its foliage. This adaptation is thought to be a mechanism for reducing water loss. The plant possesses a deep taproot, which can extend to depths of 9 to 14 feet or more. This extensive root system enables the plant to withstand drought conditions and contributes to its overall hardiness. Historically, Silphium laciniatum was utilized in Native American herbal medicine. It was employed as a vermifuge to expel intestinal parasites and was also used to treat respiratory conditions such as coughs and asthma.
